svg.text: HANDOVER — WHERE PATIENTS ARE MOST OFTEN LOST
Most serious errors begin as information that existed but never crossed a shift boundary.

g.text: Who you are, who the patient is, and what is wrong right now
"Bed 6, Mr Mensah, 54, his breathing has worsened in the last hour."
Why he is here and what is relevant — not his whole life story
"Day 3 after laparotomy, known asthmatic, on IV fluids and antibiotics."
Your observations and what you think is happening
"Resp 32, sats 88 percent on air, using accessory muscles. I think he is deteriorating."
What you want to happen, and by when — say it out loud
"Please review him within ten minutes. May I start oxygen now?"

svg.text: Nurses are often trained to hint rather than ask. "He does not look very well" leaves the listener to guess how
worried you are. State the request plainly, with a timeframe, and escalate if you do not get it.
